title: GPU operational modes and thermal profiles for inference
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures recommended operational modes (frequency/power/thermal) for common inference workload patterns and prescriptive guidance for integrating those modes into the serving runtime scheduler and KV cache placement. The goal is safe, observable, and repeatable profiles that optimize for low-tail latency, steady throughput, or cost-sensitive operation depending on the deployment tier.

Scope and context:
- GPUs covered: NVIDIA A100 (40/80GB HBM), NVIDIA H100, NVIDIA L4, AMD MI300.
- Target runtime: Redwood serving runtime kernel stack (CUTLASS/CuBLAS/TensorRT paths on NVIDIA, ROCm/hipBLAS/hipDNN on AMD).
- Workload classes: interactive short-chat (<=128 tokens), medium-context chat (256–1024 tokens), long-context batch-generation (>1024 tokens), high-throughput embedding pipelines.
- Not covered: cluster-level placement (k8s node selection) except where it impacts thermal behaviour.

Design principles / constraints:
1) Minimize tail latency variability first for latency-sensitive tiers. If necessary, trade raw throughput for predictable p99 latency.
2) Keep thermal headroom to avoid mid-run DVFS events that cause latency spikes.
3) Favor deterministic kernel paths (quantized/F16 optimized) that match the profile being run.
4) KV cache residency decisions should prioritize HBM for low-latency reuse and fall back to pinned host memory for capacity.
5) All changes must be reversible remotely and observable via telemetry exposed to Console.

Operational modes (high-level):
- latency-burst: aggressive clocks, high power cap, strong thermal headroom. For interactive endpoints with strict p99 SLOs.
- steady-throughput: moderate clocks, conservative power cap to increase efficiency/throughput over long-running batches.
- eco-saver: reduced clocks and power cap for cost-conscious background jobs (embeddings, offline evals).
- thermal-safe: emergency fallback mode when temperature/availed thermal headroom is low; reduces GPU frequency and move KV cache to host when needed.

Mode -> runtime knobs (examples):
- gpu_mode=latency-burst: set application clocks to target MHz (see per-GPU table), power_cap = 95–100% of default TDP, enable fixed SM clock if supported, pin KV cache to HBM, prefer FP16/TF32 fast-kernel path, disable runtime dynamic frequency scaling.
- gpu_mode=steady-throughput: clocks slightly below max, power_cap = 80–90% TDP, allow kernel-level boost for multi-request batching, HBM residency prioritized for hot keys only, background cache eviction allowed.
- gpu_mode=eco-saver: clocks 60–75% of base, power_cap = 60–75% TDP, favor lower-precision kernels only when quality tests pass, larger batch sizes and lower preempt priority.
- gpu_mode=thermal-safe: reduce clocks to safe_floor, power_cap = 50–70% depending on temp, move KV cache pages to pinned host memory, mark node as degraded in scheduler to avoid new pods being placed.

Per-GPU quick guidance (calibrated values are starting points; site calibration required):
- NVIDIA A100 (80GB):
  - latency-burst: application clocks ~1020–1095 MHz (SM/core) with HBM at default, power cap ~300–320W (retain vendor-recommended headroom).
  - steady-throughput: clocks ~900–1000 MHz, power cap ~250–280W.
  - eco-saver: clocks ~700–850 MHz, power cap ~180–220W.
  - notes: avoid pushing to sustained maximum clock if ambient rack temp >30C; monitor SM utilization and HBM utilization separately.

- NVIDIA H100:
  - latency-burst: enable sustained high-frequency mode where available, clocks per vendor ranges (consult firmware), power cap ~350–400W for isolated nodes.
  - steady-throughput: clocks ~85–92% of burst, power cap ~300–340W.
  - eco-saver: clocks ~65–80% of burst, power cap ~220–270W.
  - notes: H100 has more aggressive thermal rollback behaviour; prefer pre-warming and conservative headroom if SLO-critical.

- NVIDIA L4 (edge/inference-focused):
  - latency-burst: set clock to max-perf state allowed by driver, power cap at device default (approx 45–60W depending on SKUs).
  - steady-throughput: modest clocks and small batch accumulation (2–8) to amortize kernel launches.
  - eco-saver: drop to lower-power state and increase batching; migrate large KV items to host memory if HBM constrained.
  - notes: L4 is optimized for INT8/FP16; prefer these kernels where quality is acceptable.

- AMD MI300:
  - latency-burst: use highest supported XGMI/mesh clocks and HBM freq, power cap near vendor defaults for single-tenant nodes.
  - steady-throughput: moderate clocks and allow ROCm power-management to smooth frequencies across compute units.
  - eco-saver: lower clocks, increase batch sizes.
  - notes: ROCm telemetry exposes temperature per chiplet; ensure cross-chiplet KV coherence when evicting to host.

KV cache placement and thermal interaction:
- Principle: KV reads must be fast for hot prefixes. HBM-resident KV gives best p99, but consumes memory and may cause thermal pressure.
- Hot-shard policy: pin top N% hot keys to HBM (N tuned per model and GPU type). For latency-burst mode N is higher (e.g., 80–90%). For steady-throughput N is moderate (40–60%). For eco-saver N may be 10–20% or none.
- Eviction triggers: free HBM below threshold (e.g., 85% occupancy) or when GPU thermal headroom < 10% (to avoid DVFS bounce). Eviction should prefer moving entire KV segments to pinned host memory rather than partial fragments to avoid extra GPU-host trips.
- Prefetching: Predictive prefetch of KV based on session activity should be conservative on L4/MI300 if temperature is trending up.

Kernel selection and affinity:
- Bind kernels to stable execution paths: for short sequences prefer single-token generation optimized kernels with small-launch overhead. For long tokens prefer tiled matmul kernels.
- On NVIDIA: prefer CUTLASS+TensorRT fused kernels for FP16/INT8; disable fallback JIT paths in latency-burst mode to avoid unexpected codegen variability.
- On AMD: fix rocBLAS/hipDNN versions in the runtime image and pin to tested kernel builds.
- Affinity: where multiple GPUs share PCIe switches, prefer co-locating chat sessions with their KV on the same GPU to avoid cross-PCIe traffic that increases temp and latency.

Thermal policies and thresholds (operational):
- Temperature thresholds (example):
  - temp_warn = 75C (increase telemetry sampling frequency, log warning)
  - temp_soft_limit = 82–85C (enter thermal-safe if sustained >30s)
  - temp_hard_limit = 90–95C (force throttling and notify operators)
- Fan and chassis notes: On cloud instances fan control is often managed by provider; do not attempt aggressive fan overrides without provider agreement. For on-prem racks, use conservative fan curves to reduce acoustic ingress spikes and allow steady cooling.
- Thermal hysteresis: require sustained crossing of threshold for 20–30s before switching modes to avoid flapping.

Scheduler integration (runtime):
- Expose gpu_mode as a route-level config flag plus an automatic selector. Automatic selection is based on recent request latency distribution, request size histogram, and current thermal headroom.
- Route config example flags: gpu_mode, max_batch_size_override, kv_hot_pct_target, allow_quantized_kernels.
- Admission control: if node is in thermal-safe mode, runtime should mark capacity as degraded and avoid scheduling new latency-critical routes there.

Telemetry and metrics to collect (minimum):
- GPU temp (per GPU), power draw (W), SM/compute utilization, HBM usage, PCIe bandwidth, per-kernel latency histogram, p50/p95/p99 request latency, KV hit ratio, number of KV page migrations to host.
- Emit events on mode transitions with cause labels (manual, telemetry-driven, provider thermal event).

Testing and calibration plan:
- Step 1: baseline profiling across all GPUs with standard microbench (single-token generation, 8-token burst, long-context stream).
- Step 2: run 24–48h thermal soak tests at latency-burst settings to observe real thermal rollback points.
- Step 3: sweep power caps in 5% increments to build perf vs power curves and identify knee points for each workload class.
- Step 4: KV cache stress test: synthetic hot-key skew and then see eviction behaviour and p99 impact.
- Step 5: run canary routes in production with telemetry gates before global rollout.

Operational checklist for rollout:
- Update runtime to expose gpu_mode and related knobs in Console.
- Add telemetry dashboards: per-node thermal profile, mode transition log, KV residency heatmap.
- Run calibration sweep and store per-cluster profile in configuration service.
- Create a rollback playbook: revert to previous power/clock settings, drain node, and mark node unhealthy.

Known risks and mitigations:
- Risk: pushing clocks/power without adequate thermal headroom causes mid-run DVFS and p99 spikes. Mitigation: use conservative headroom thresholds and require sustained warm-up before enabling latency-burst.
- Risk: evicting KV to host increases PCIe traffic causing thermal rise and latency. Mitigation: batch host transfers during low-load windows and prefer moving whole segments.
- Risk: provider-managed firmware or driver updates change clock semantics. Mitigation: pin driver/FW in AMIs and validate on smoke tests.

Next steps / action items:
- Run calibration matrix for one representative cluster per GPU family (owners: Diego & Owen).
- Implement gpu_mode flags and KV hot-shard target in runtime (owner: Priya).
- Add Console widgets for thermal mode transitions and KV residency (owner: Maya).
- Draft operator runbook for emergency thermal events (owner: SRE oncall).

Appendix: quick checklist for SREs when investigating p99 spikes:
- Check GPU temp/time-series and recent mode transitions.
- Confirm KV hit rate; if suddenly lower, examine eviction logs.
- Verify driver/firmware didn’t change recently via linked_artifacts.
- If thermal rollback visible, either: increase mode headroom, reduce incoming request rate, or move routes off the node.

End of document
